chunks: And from him from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Idris al-Qummi who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Indeed, a freedman of ours performed Tamattu' (pilgratitude with Umrah then Hajj), and when he shaved his head, he put on clothes before visiting the House (Kaaba).' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there any blame upon him?' He said: 'No.' I said: 'For I saw Ibn Abi Sammak running between Safa and Marwah, wearing two socks, a qaba' (tunic), and a belt.' He said: 'What a bad thing he did.' I said: 'Is there any blame upon him?' He said: 'No.'

The explanation in these two narrations is that they came at the place of recommendation and preference, not prohibition and obligation, because it is recommended that the pilgrim does not return to the rulings of those who are free from restrictions except after completing all his rituals, so that his heart does not become occupied with performing what is obligatory upon him, and if he did it, there is no blame upon him. And that which indicates that they came on the path of recommendation is what has been narrated:

key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةِ: Safa and Marwah (the hills between which pilgrims walk)
key_terms.تَمَتَّعَ: Performed Tamattu' Hajj (combining Umrah and Hajj)

ai.seo_question: Is it forbidden for a pilgrim to wear clothes before completing Hajj rituals?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that donning regular clothes or performing acts of the free state before completing all Hajj rituals is recommended (mustahabb) rather than obligatory or prohibited, ensuring the pilgrim’s heart remains fully engaged in the rites. This ruling, derived from the phrase 'bisa ma sana'a' (what he did was good), reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on spiritual focus (khushu') during the transition from ihram to the final state of freedom, a principle rooted in the Quranic injunction to complete the pilgrimage. The hadith underscores that while premature actions do not invalidate the Hajj, delaying them aligns with the ideal of uninterrupted devotion.
